desc:
Count the paths of a binary tree whose node values add up to target, where a path is allowed to start at any node and end at any node below it. It always moves from a parent to one of its children, never upward. A path consists of at least one node, and it does not need to start at the root or end at a leaf.

Two paths are different if their sets of nodes differ, even when the values are identical. Node values can be negative or zero, so several different start nodes can combine with the same end node.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). Node values can be negative in this problem, so a missing child is written as 1000 (real node values always lie between -500 and 500, so the marker can never be confused with a value). The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing 1000 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with 1000. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, 1000, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [10, 5, -3, 3, 2, 1000, 11, 3, -2, 1000, 1] and target = 8 the answer is 3: the paths 5 → 3, 5 → 2 → 1 and -3 → 11.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, missing child written as 1000, no trailing 1000)
The answer fits in a 32-bit integer (it is at most 1,500 · 1,501 / 2)
hints: Fix the end node of a path instead of the start. Which start nodes make the path sum equal target?
If S(v) is the sum from the root to v, a downward path from an ancestor u (its child side) to v has sum S(v) - S(parent(u)). So you need ancestors whose prefix sum is exactly S(v) - target.

Keep a hash map counting the prefix sums on the current root-to-node path (start with {0: 1}). On entering a node, add count[S - target] to the answer, then record S; on leaving the node, remove it again.
editorial: Checking every start node costs O(n · depth), which is up to O(n2) on a chain. The standard trick from subarray sums carries over to trees: let S(v) be the sum of values from the root to v. A downward path that ends at v and starts at a proper descendant of an ancestor a has sum S(v) - S(a). It equals target exactly when S(a) = S(v) - target, where a may also be the virtual prefix 0 before the root.

So run a DFS that maintains a map from prefix sum to the number of ancestors (on the current path) with that prefix sum, initialised with {0: 1}. When you enter v compute S(v), add map[S(v) - target] to the answer, then increment map[S(v)]. When you leave v, decrement it again so the map only ever describes the current root-to-node path. Use an explicit stack with enter and exit markers because the tree can be 1,500 deep.
Every node is entered and left once: O(n) time and O(depth) extra space for the map.
